summary:
Mars Explorer AI — Integrated Martian Map is an interactive bilingual research prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge.

The project brings together NASA Mars Trek cartographic layers, including MOLA elevation visualization and HiRISE imagery of Jezero Crater, with experimental terrain-analysis and pathfinding research.

Users can explore Martian surface imagery, examine the Perseverance landing location, switch between map layers, and compare A* and Dijkstra algorithms using results from our Kaggle research archive of 70 experiments.

The prototype combines planetary mapping, reproducible research evidence, and accessible visualization to demonstrate how different scientific resources can support future exploration planning.

Our research began before the hackathon; the interactive map is a separate demonstration of that earlier work. Route comparisons are experimental and are not independently georeferenced to the Jezero map. Geological polygons, coordinate-registration accuracy, and physical traversal safety have not yet been validated.

The project is publicly available through GitHub Pages, with source code and research documentation on GitHub and Kaggle.
details:
Mars Explorer AI — Integrated Martian Map

Team: MarsWay UA
Challenge: Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

1. Project Concept and Purpose

Mars Explorer AI is a bilingual interactive research prototype that combines NASA planetary imagery, Martian terrain visualization, scientific data provenance, and experimental route-planning research in a single public web application.

The project addresses a key challenge in future Mars exploration: understanding the terrain, identifying relevant scientific information, and comparing exploration-planning approaches using accessible and traceable data.

Our objective is to demonstrate how NASA resources and computational research can be brought together to support scientific interpretation, education, and the development of future exploration-planning tools.

2. How the System Works

The application provides four interconnected research sections.

Jezero Overview: An interactive schematic overview showing the Perseverance landing location, study-region boundaries, and contextual information about Jezero Crater.

Pathfinding Demonstration: A synthetic grid-based environment for exploring route planning with A* and Dijkstra algorithms. This section demonstrates algorithmic behavior and is not a validated physical navigation system.

Kaggle Research Evidence: Research results derived from a broader archive of 70 Kaggle notebooks covering Martian imagery, machine learning, terrain analysis, uncertainty, reproducibility, and route-planning algorithms.

NASA Mars Trek Integration: Interactive NASA map tiles, including MGS MOLA color hillshade and the MRO HiRISE Jezero controlled mosaic, with map-layer selection and exploration controls.

The interface is available in English and Ukrainian.

3. NASA Data and Scientific Resources

The project uses NASA Mars Trek mapping services to display authentic planetary cartographic imagery.

The MOLA layer provides regional and global terrain context, while the HiRISE controlled mosaic offers a more detailed orbital view of Jezero Crater.

The application also includes the published Perseverance landing-site coordinates and references the USGS SIM 3464 geological map.

A geological GeoJSON import interface is available, but actual geological polygons have not yet been integrated into the released application.

4. Artificial Intelligence and Computational Research

The project builds on a research program comprising 70 historical Kaggle experiments organized into six phases.

The research covers image classification with convolutional neural networks, digital terrain model processing, algorithmic route planning, terrain-related uncertainty, source-data provenance, and reproducibility.

The interactive application incorporates research outputs from experiment v026, including comparisons of A* and Dijkstra across seven research windows and two conditional slope-margin settings.

These research results are displayed separately from the NASA cartographic layers because independent spatial alignment has not been established.

5. Technologies and Implementation

The public prototype is implemented with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and is hosted through GitHub Pages.

Python and Jupyter notebooks were used in the underlying Kaggle research workflows. Research artifacts include structured CSV files, JSON metadata, SHA-256 integrity manifests, and audit documentation.

The project uses public NASA mapping resources, the GitHub source-code repository, and the Kaggle research archive.

6. Innovation and Benefits

The distinctive contribution of Mars Explorer AI is not a claim of autonomous rover navigation, but the integration of planetary imagery, experimental algorithmic evidence, and transparent scientific limitations in one accessible research environment.

The system helps users explore Jezero Crater, understand differences between route-planning algorithms, inspect research evidence, and trace the origins of the displayed information.

Its bilingual interface also supports broader educational access to planetary science and computational methods.

7. Validation and Scientific Limitations

The public release includes locally checked research datasets and integrity documentation. The interactive map has been tested in a web browser with NASA MOLA and HiRISE imagery successfully displayed.

However, independent geodetic control points, coordinate-registration accuracy, geological polygon integration, terrain-slope uncertainty, and physical route safety have not been validated.

The prototype must not be used for operational rover navigation or human Mars traversal.

8. Expected Impact and Future Development

Future work will focus on more rigorous spatial registration, additional geological and terrain datasets, improved uncertainty modelling, independently validated geographic overlays, and closer integration of machine-learning outputs with mapped study areas.

Mars Explorer AI demonstrates how an open, reproducible, and transparent research workflow can evolve into an interactive foundation for future Martian exploration-support tools.

Source code: https://github.com/oleksisa/mars-explorer-ai-martian-map
